content: The use of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir with other proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) has not been studied, so close monitoring is recommended. Sodium bicarbonate can reduce sotalol levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption, which applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and separate administration by at least 2 hours. Omeprazole decreases the levels and effects of sotorasib by reducing gastrointestinal absorption; this interaction applies only to oral forms. Avoid or use alternative drugs. If co-administration with an acid-reducing agent is unavoidable, administer sotorasib 4 hours before or 10 hours after a locally-acting antacid. Sparsentan reduces omeprazole levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C19 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. Omeprazole decreases sparsentan efficacy by increasing gastric pH, which applies only to oral forms. St. John’s Wort decreases omeprazole levels by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Monitor closely. Stiripentol, a CYP3A4 inhibitor and inducer, increases omeprazole levels by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism. Adjust therapy and monitor closely. Consider reducing the dose of CYP2C19 substrates if adverse reactions occur when co-administered with stiripentol. Sodium bicarbonate reduces strontium ranelate levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption, which applies only to oral forms. Separate administration by 2 hours when possible. Sodium bicarbonate also affects sulfasalazine through passive renal tubular reabsorption due to increased pH, with salicylate levels increasing at moderate doses and decreasing at high doses. Monitor closely. Omeprazole increases tacrolimus levels by affecting CYP2C19 metabolism, particularly in intermediate or poor metabolizers. Monitor whole blood concentrations closely. Tazemetostat decreases omeprazole levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, while omeprazole increases tazemetostat levels. Use caution and monitor closely. Sodium bicarbonate reduces tetracycline levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Avoid or use alternative drugs, separating administration by 2 hours. Omeprazole increases the toxicity of theophylline due to prolonged PPI use, which can cause hypochlorhydria and alter intestinal motility. Monitor for toxicity. Omeprazole decreases thyroid desiccated levels by increasing gastric pH, with conflicting evidence regarding this interaction. Monitor closely. Sodium bicarbonate reduces tiludronate levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Separate administration by 2 hours and monitor closely. Sodium bicarbonate also reduces timolol levels by the same mechanism. Separate by 2 hours and monitor closely. Omeprazole increases tinidazole levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor closely. Omeprazole also increases tofacitinib levels via CYP2C19 metabolism. No specific dose adjustment is recommended unless co-administered with both moderate CYP3A4 and potent CYP2C19 inhibitors. Sodium bicarbonate reduces trandolapril effects through an unspecified mechanism. Use caution and monitor. Omeprazole increases triazolam levels by decreasing metabolism. Monitor closely. Triclabendazole increases omeprazole levels via CYP2C19 metabolism. Use caution and monitor. Tucatinib increases omeprazole levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid or use alternative drugs, as tucatinib with CYP3A substrates may lead to serious toxicities. If unavoidable, reduce the CYP3A substrate dose per product labeling. Sodium bicarbonate reduces ursodiol effects through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Monitor closely. Omeprazole decreases vismodegib levels by altering gastric pH, which reduces solubility and bioavailability. Monitor closely. Voriconazole increases omeprazole levels via CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor closely. Omeprazole increases warfarin levels by affecting the metabolism of its R-enantiomer through CYP3A4, CYP1A2, and CYP2C19. Monitor INR more frequently and adjust the warfarin dose if needed. Sodium bicarbonate affects willow bark through passive renal tubular reabsorption due to increased pH, with salicylate levels varying by dose. Monitor closely. Sodium bicarbonate reduces zoledronic acid levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Separate administration by 2 hours and monitor closely. Common adverse effects include pyrexia (20%), hypokalemia (12%), hyperglycemia (11%), nosocomial pneumonia (11%), hypotension (10%), hypomagnesemia (10%), hypertension (8%), atrial fibrillation (6%), hypocalcemia (6%), rash (6%), tachycardia (5%), constipation (5%), sepsis (5%), hyperpyrexia (5%), oral candidiasis (4%), bradycardia (4%), diarrhea (4%), edema (3%), supraventricular tachycardia (3%), decubitus ulcer (3%), agitation (3%), hypernatremia (2%), hyperkalemia (2%), urinary tract infection (2%), hypomotility (2%), and candidal infection (2%). Rare effects include angina, fractures, glycosuria, anemia, hepatic failure, benign gastric polyps, agranulocytosis, alopecia, increased creatinine, hemolytic anemia, angioedema, gynecomastia, anorexia, hepatic encephalopathy, metabolic alkalosis, pancreatitis, photosensitivity, liver disease, lupus erythematosus, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea, fundic gland polyps, acute interstitial nephritis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) may cause atrophic gastritis, acute interstitial nephritis, and increased risk of Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD). Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration. PPIs are associated with cutaneous and systemic lupus erythematosus, which typically resolves within 4–12 weeks after discontinuation. Long-term use may increase the risk of osteoporosis-related fractures, fundic gland polyps, and gastric atrophy. Relief of symptoms does not eliminate the possibility of gastric malignancy; consider additional diagnostic testing for suboptimal responses or early relapses. Therapy may increase the risk of infections such as Salmonella and Campylobacter. PPIs may require dosage adjustments in liver disease and have increased bioavailability in the elderly. Animal studies suggest a potential risk of gastric carcinoid tumors, but human risk is unconfirmed. PPIs are present in human milk, but their effects on breastfed infants are unknown. Consider the benefits of breastfeeding alongside the mother’s clinical needs and potential adverse effects. There are no adequate studies in pregnant women, but available data suggest no evidence of fetal risk.
